nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-01.title: Inclusion–exclusion
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-01.body:
From $1$ to $100$: $25$ multiples of $4$, $20$ multiples of $5$, and $5$ multiples of $20$ (counted twice). So $25+20-5=40$.

**Answer: 40**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-01.title: Count per block of 20
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-01.body:
In each block of $20$ consecutive integers, the multiples of $4$ or $5$ are $5+4-1=8$ numbers. The numbers $1$ to $100$ form $5$ such blocks: $5\cdot8=40$.

**Answer: 40**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-02.title: Self-similarity
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-02.body:
Let $x$ be the value. The expression under the outer root is $5+x$, so $x^2=5+x$, i.e. $x^2-x-5=0$. Taking the positive root, $x=\frac{1+\sqrt{21}}{2}$, so $a=21$, $b=1$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt{21}+1}{2}$**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-03.title: Parity
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-03.body:
$25q+10d=185$. Since $10d$ is even and $185$ is odd, $q$ is odd. $q=1$ works ($185=25+16\cdot10$), and $q=7$ works ($185=175+10$), while $q=9$ is too large. The difference is $7-1=6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-04.title: Common base
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-04.body:
Writing everything as powers of $3$: $3^{x^2}\cdot3^{-6x}=3^{-9}$, so $x^2-6x=-9$, i.e. $(x-3)^2=0$. The only solution is $x=3$.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-05.title: Cube root
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-05.body:
$216000=60^3$. A cube $k^3$ divides $60^3$ exactly when $k$ divides $60$, and $60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5$ has $3\cdot2\cdot2=12$ divisors.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-06.title: Set up the ratios
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-06.body:
Let $QU=3k$, $DQ=2k$, $UA=h$. Both triangles are right: $[QUA]=\frac12\cdot3k\cdot h$ and $[QDA]=\frac12\cdot2k\cdot15=15k$. Their ratio is $\frac{3kh/2}{15k}=\frac{h}{10}=\frac{9}{10}$, so $h=9$. Then $QU=\sqrt{15^2-9^2}=12$, $k=4$, $DQ=8$. The area is $\frac12\cdot12\cdot9+\frac12\cdot8\cdot15=54+60=114$.

**Answer: 114**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-07.title: Check in order
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-07.body:
The prime digits are $2,3,5,7$. The smallest candidates start with $2$: $235$ (divisible by $5$), $237$ (digit sum $12$, divisible by $3$), $253=11\cdot23$, $257$. Testing $257$ against the primes up to $\sqrt{257}\approx16$ ($2,3,5,7,11,13$) shows it is prime.

**Answer: 257**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-08.title: Quadratic formula
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-08.body:
The roots are $\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4c}}{2}$, so their difference is $\sqrt{b^2-4c}=8$ and $b^2-4c=64$.

**Answer: 64**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-09.title: Middle number
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-09.body:
The middle (51st) number is the average, $\frac{50500}{101}=500$. The greatest is $50$ more: $550$.

**Answer: 550**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-10.title: Product of slopes
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-10.body:
The slopes are $-(m+2)$ and $-(m-2)$. Perpendicular lines have slopes with product $-1$: $(m+2)(m-2)=-1$, so $m^2=3$ and $m=\pm\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $\pm\sqrt3$**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-11.title: One equation
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-11.body:
Let Sam be $S$, so Pat is $2S$. Then $S-3=\frac{2S+5}{3}$, so $3S-9=2S+5$ and $S=14$. Check: $11$ is a third of $33=28+5$.

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-12.title: Equal times
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-12.body:
Let Babu's speed be $v$, so Abu's is $1.25v$ and Abu finishes in $\frac{5}{1.25v}=\frac4v$. If Babu jumps after $m$ miles, the boat takes $\frac mv+\frac{5-m}{2v}$. Setting these equal: $2m+5-m=8$, so $m=3$.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-12.title: Pick a speed
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-12.body:
Say Babu and Cabu row $4$ mph, so Abu rows $5$ mph and finishes in $1$ hour. In that hour the shared boat covers $m$ miles at $4$ mph and $5-m$ at $8$ mph: $\frac m4+\frac{5-m}8=1$, i.e. $2m+5-m=8$, $m=3$.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-13.title: Two-digit case
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-13.body:
A one-digit $n$ would satisfy $n=2n$, impossible. A number with $k\ge3$ digits is at least $10^{k-1}$, far more than $2\cdot9k$. For two digits $\overline{AB}$: $10A+B=2A+2B$ gives $B=8A$, so $A=1$, $B=8$: the number is $18$.

**Answer: 18**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-14.title: Distance from the center
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-14.body:
The center $(4,2)$ is at distance $\frac{|3\cdot4+4\cdot2-45|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=\frac{25}{5}=5$ from the line. The radius is $3$, so the gap between the circle and the line is $5-3=2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-14.title: Foot of the perpendicular
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-14.body:
The perpendicular from $(4,2)$ has slope $\frac43$; it meets $3x+4y=45$ at $(7,6)$, at distance $\sqrt{9+16}=5$ from the center. Subtracting the radius $3$ leaves $2$.

**Answer: 2**

nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-17.title: Groups of 24
nyciml-2014-15-spring-sophfrosh-17.body:
A multiple $6k$ is also a multiple of $8$ exactly when $4\mid k$. So in each block of $4$ consecutive values of $k$ (each block of $24$ numbers), $3$ are on the list. The first $33$ blocks ($k=1,\dots,132$) contain $99$ list members. The next list member is $k=133$, so the 100th number is $6\cdot133=798$.

**Answer: 798**
